Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Gestural relativity of spatial cognition: Gesture can express and transmit the spatial frames of reference that structure thinking

text.text: When people think spatially, they adopt a frame of reference (egocentric or allocentric).
People within a community often rely on the same frame of reference, but there is considerable variation between communities.
How are these norms of spatial thinking transmitted?
Linguistic relativity posits that they are transmitted through language; evidence for this account is mixed.
We investigate a complementary mechanism, gestural relativity, whereby norms of spatial thinking are transmitted by gestures that express spatial information.
Experiment 1 (N = 62 US Americans) tested whether exposure to a norm favoring a particular frame of reference causes people to adopt that frame of reference in their gestures.
Experiment 2 (N = 70) tested whether observing such gestures causes people to adopt that frame of reference in their spatial reasoning.
We find evidence for both effects.
Gesture can thus express and transmit spatial frames of reference, establishing gesture as a viable mechanism of cultural transmission.
Reasoning about space is mostly a private affair.
When we plan routes, remember where we left our keys, or imagine the layout of a room, our mental representations are invisible to others.
Yet spatial thinking is not entirely idiosyncratic.
Within communities, people converge on shared ways of thinking about space.
These norms are seldom explicitly taught and yet somehow are maintained and transmitted.
How do private habits of spatial thinking become public and shared?
Spatial frames of reference are a canonical example of this puzzle.
A computer mouse, for instance, could simultaneously lie to the left and to the north of a keyboard.
These descriptions reflect different ways of organizing space in a particular spatial frame of reference (FoR).
The first anchors the spatial coordinate system to the speaker's body in an egocentric FoR.
The second anchors it to external features of the world in an allocentric FoR.
Many communities favor one over the other.

Speakers of English and Spanish, for instance, default to egocentric descriptions of small-scale space, while speakers of Tzeltal and Guugu Yimithirr prefer allocentric ones (Haviland, 1993; Brown & Levinson, 1993; Levinson, 2003; Calderón et al., 2019).

text.text: These preferences manifest not only in language but also in memory and reasoning (Majid et al., 2004).

text.text: This community-wide convergence on shared preferences for spatial frames of reference is striking, since the underlying cognitive convention is rarely taught explicitly.
Some public channel must be conveying this private practice.

One account of these shared spatial norms is linguistic relativity (Whorf, 1956; Levinson, 2003; Majid et al., 2004), the proposal that habitually using a particular frame of reference in language causes community members to preferentially adopt that frame of reference in non-linguistic thought.
text.formatted: One account of these shared spatial norms is linguistic relativity <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Whorf, 1956;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Levinson, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Majid et al., 2004)</ref>, the proposal that habitually using a particular frame of reference in language causes community members to preferentially adopt that frame of reference in non-linguistic thought.

text.text: On this account, spatial descriptions produced or encountered within a community function as cues that nudge speakers and listeners toward thinking spatially in a particular way.
Through repeated exposure, these cues stabilize into durable cognitive habits.

Evidence for this account comes from cross-cultural correlations between language and non-linguistic thinking: Communities that habitually describe space egocentrically also tend to remember and reason egocentrically, while communities that describe space allocentrically tend to remember and reason allocentrically (Levinson, 1996; Levinson, 2003; Majid et al., 2004).

text.text: But linguistic relativity can't be the whole story, since a community's spatial language sometimes diverges from its spatial thought (Le Guen, 2011; Adamou & Shen, 2017; Calderón et al., 2019; Kısa et al., 2026).

text.text: Linguistic relativity cannot explain these dissociations between spatial language and spatial thought.
Communities must have additional channels by which shared spatial conventions are expressed and transmitted.
Here we investigate one such channel: gesture.
Gesture has properties that make it a particularly potent vehicle for transmitting a community's norms for adopting a frame of reference in spatial thinking.
First, gesture is intrinsically spatial.
Gestures are enacted in space and are thus natural vehicles for information about movement and spatial relationships.

Indeed, people are more likely to gesture when thinking about and communicating spatial information (Alibali, 2005; Hostetter & Alibali, 2008), and gestures can express fine-grained spatial information not available in speech (Cook & Tanenhaus, 2009).

text.text: Second, the spatial frame of reference adopted in gesture has been claimed to align with the normative frame of reference in a speaker's community (Haviland, 1993), although so far the evidence for this claim has been qualitative and correlational.

text.text: Third, gesture has been shown to influence thinking about other aspects of space (e.g., Kita et al., 2017; Alibali, 2005; Zhang et al., 2024; Van Wermeskerken et al., 2016; Kang & Tversky, 2016) and about other conceptual domains such as time (Tversky & Jamalian, 2021; Lewis & Stickles, 2017) and mathematics (Singer & Goldin-Meadow, 2005; Lorson et al., 2025).

text.text: Fourth, and critically, a few studies have found that the frame of reference adopted in gesture matches the frame of reference adopted for non-communicative spatial thinking, even when the frame of reference adopted in speech is entirely different (e.g., Yucatec Maya women, Le Guen, 2011; Ngigua-Spanish bilinguals, Calderón et al., 2019).

text.text: The evidence for a link between gesture and community-level FoR norms, however, has thus far been correlational.

We lack evidence of a causal connection between gesture and norms of spatial thought -a problem also faced by much of the evidence for linguistic relativity of spatial frames of reference (Marghetis et al., 2020; Pitt et al., 2022).

text.text: If gesture is to function as a channel by which spatial norms are maintained within a community, then two complementary processes must occur.
First, speakers' gestures should reliably express local norms for spatial thinking.

If members of a community prefer to think about space egocentrically, then this should cause them to gesture more egocentrically; if they prefer to think allocentrically, then this should cause them to gesture more allocentrically.
Second, people who observe these gestures should adopt the encoded frame of reference in their own reasoning.
If both processes occur, then gesture would be a viable channel by which implicit spatial conventions are made public and transmitted within a community.
We refer to this hypothesis as the gestural relativity of spatial cognition.
Here, we test both processes.
In Experiment 1, we manipulated the frame of reference that groups used normatively to reason non-linguistically about small-scale space.
We then investigated whether people in those groups spontaneously adopted that normative frame of reference in their subsequent gestures.
In Experiment 2, we manipulated the frame of reference that a researcher used in their gestures to describe small-scale space.
We then investigated whether participants adopted that frame of reference in their own spatial reasoning.
Together, these two experiments test the viability of gestural relativity as a mechanism for the cultural transmission of norms of spatial thinking.

In a between-subjects design, we implicitly manipulated the normative frame of reference for spatial reasoning (egocentric vs. allocentric) using a social learning paradigm.
Participants completed two rotation-based spatial tasks: a Cup Task and a Map Task.
For each task, they first completed a Training phase, followed by a Test phase (Fig. 1).

text.text: Here we describe the overall design, which was the same for both tasks.
In the next section we describe the procedural details for the Cup and Map tasks, which both measure reasoning about small-scale spatial relationships.
The Training phase for each task was designed to transmit the local norm for spatial reasoning through observation and social learning, without explicit references to a particular frame of reference.
On each Training trial (n = 4 trials/task), an experimenter (the "Director") demonstrated a spatial movement on a table.
This movement was observed by the participant and a second experimenter (the "Player").
All three then rotated 180° to a second, identical table, and the Director asked them to reproduce the motion "the same way" on this second table.

After the rotation, egocentric and allocentric strategies yield contrasting responses: an egocentric solution reproduces motion trajectories from the observer's perspective (e.g., a motion to their left), while an allocentric solution preserves them relative to external coordinates, so a motion that was originally observed going from left-to-right should be reproduced going from right-to-left (i.e., maintaining the motion's absolute orientation).
On the first Training trial, only the Player attempted to recreate the Director's motion, modeling the normative frame of reference for the participant.
On subsequent Training trials, both the participant and the Player attempted to reproduce the Director's motion, in that order.

If the participant's response did not reproduce the Director's motion trajectory according to the local norm (i.e., egocentrically or allocentrically), the Director provided generic verbal feedback, saying, "No you moved it differently, [the Player] did it correctly.
Make sure you move it the same way."
The assigned frame of reference was never named or described explicitly; it was conveyed only through the Player's behavior and the Director's feedback.
Researchers never gestured.
The Test phase was designed to investigate whether participants, having learned the local norm, would spontaneously convey that norm in their gestures.
On each trial of the Test Phase (n = 4 trials per task), the participant adopted the role of the Director and improvised a motion trajectory.
Unlike the Training trials, during the Test trials the Player turned away so they could not see the motion.
Participant and Player then rotated to face each other and the participant described the motion trajectory to the Player.
The Player then turned 180º to an identical table where they attempted to reproduce the participant's motion based on their description.
An occluding barrier was inserted between the tables to ensure that participants received no visual feedback from the Player's motion on the second table.
Participants were never encouraged to gesture.

Critically, for each Test trial, we analyzed whether the participant gestured during their description of the motion trajectory and, if so, whether their gestures adopted an egocentric or allocentric FoR.
Participants' descriptions were coded online by the Director and also video-recorded for offline reliability coding.
During each Test trial, the Director noted whether the participant used their hands or head to convey the motion trajectory, and if so, the primary direction of these gestures.

If the primary direction of gestures on a trial was consistent with the participant's egocentric perspective (e.g., a leftward motion was conveyed by a leftward gesture), the gesture for that trial was categorized as egocentric.

If the primary direction was consistent with an external frame of reference (e.g., a motion toward the wall was conveyed by a gesture toward the wall), the gesture for that trial was categorized as allocentric.

Trials in which the gestures lacked any lateral motion component (n = 11) and trials in which gestures conveyed motion in both lateral directions (n = 4) were coded as neither egocentric nor allocentric.
To assess reliability of the online coding, a researcher who was not present for data collection re-coded 20% of participants from video-recordings.
Interrater reliability was high (Cohen's kappa: κ = .87).

After completing both tasks, participants answered a series of demographic and individual difference questions (e.g., gender, age, language use, urban/rural environments they grew up in, and ability to judge cardinal directions).

While the overall design was identical for the Cup and Map tasks, each task used a different procedure to probe spatial reasoning.
Task order was fixed (Cup Task then Map Task).
For each task, we used a fixed list of items, with list order counterbalanced across participants (Fig 1).

text.text: Here we describe the procedural details for each task.
The Cup task involved reproducing the motion of a small ball.
Both tables had four cups in a row and a small ball.
On a trial, a ball was first moved through the air from one cup to another (e.g., by tracing a zig-zag motion).
The task then consisted of trying to reproduce this motion trajectory on a second table.
During the Training Phase, the Director used preset trajectories for the ball, with the primary directionleftward or rightward -manipulated between trials (Fig. 1A/1B).
text.formatted: During the Training Phase, the Director used preset trajectories for the ball, with the primary directionleftward or rightward -manipulated between trials (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A/1B</ref>).

text.text: During the Test Phase, the participant was free to improvise the ball's trajectory from one of the outermost cups to the other outermost cup.
The Map task involved reproducing an exit route from a maze with multiple possible exit routes.
Both tables had identical mazes that were symmetric under 180° rotation.
The map on the first table had a prescribed route marked with a blue line.
The map on the second table was identical but the prescribed route was unmarked.
The task consisted of trying to reproduce the prescribed route on the second table.
The routes consisted primarily of motion along the lateral axis, with the primary direction -leftward or rightward -manipulated between trials (Fig. 1C/1D).

text.text: Critically, both tasks can be completed in two ways: egocentrically or allocentrically.
The egocentric solution involves anchoring spatial relations to the observer's own body.
For instance, participants could reproduce a map escape route on the second table using the same sequence of motions from their perspective.
The allocentric solution involves anchoring spatial relations to external coordinates.
For instance, participants could reproduce a map escape route on the second table using movements anchored to the room's layout (e.g., moving away or toward a salient wall).
While neither solution is "wrong" in any objective sense, the Training phase conveyed implicitly that a particular frame of reference was normative in the local context.
We analyzed the spatial frame of reference adopted in participants' gestures (egocentric or allocentric) during their Test phase descriptions.
We fit a multilevel Bayesian logistic model for each spatial frame of reference (egocentric or allocentric).

For each trial on which participants gestured, the model predicted whether they adopted that frame of reference, with fixed effects of the norm condition (allocentric or egocentric, dummy coded), task (Cup or Map, contrast coded), their interaction, and by-participant random intercepts.
Models were fit in R using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) with default priors.

text.text: We next investigated whether participants adopted a consistent frame of reference in their gestures while describing motion.
We identified each participant's predominant frame of reference as the one they adopted on the most trials.
Participants were internally consistent in their adoption of a particular frame of reference.
On trials where participants encoded a frame of reference in gesture, they adopted their predominant frame of reference 77% of the time, on average.

This consistency is much higher than expected by chance: We simulated the experiment (N = 10,000 replicates), with 62 participants randomly selecting an egocentric or allocentric FoR on each of eight trials; the mean internal-consistency in FoR was greater in the empirically-observed sample than in every single simulated run.
We next addressed our main question: whether the local norm for spatial thinking shaped how participants gestured spontaneously while describing motion events.
As predicted, participants' gestures were shaped systematically by the local norm for spatial thinking that was modeled during training (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: As predicted, participants' gestures were shaped systematically by the local norm for spatial thinking that was modeled during training (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Participants exposed to an egocentric norm were more likely to gesture about spatial relationships egocentrically (proportion of trials with gesture: M = .73 ± .04 SEM) than allocentrically (M = .26 ± .04 SEM).

Participants exposed to an allocentric norm, by comparison, produced fewer egocentric gestures (M = .52 ± .05 SEM) and more allocentric gestures (M = .40 ± .05 SEM) than those in the egocentric condition, although they still exhibited an overall egocentric bias.
Brief exposure to a local norm for spatial thinking, therefore, shaped how participants encoded motion events in their spontaneous gestures.
This effect of the local spatial norm was confirmed by multilevel Bayesian logistic models of the frame of reference adopted in gesture.
We fit two models, one of whether participants gestured egocentrically on each trial, and one of whether they gestured allocentrically (see Methods).

Compared to participants exposed to the allocentric norm, participants exposed to the egocentric norm were reliably more likely to gesture egocentrically (b = 1.14, 95% Bayesian Credible Interval = [0.27, 2.07]) but less likely to gesture allocentrically (b = -0.93, 95% BCI = [-1.84, -0.12]).

These effects were consistent across both tasks (Condition x Task in the model of egocentric responses: b = -0.06, 95% BCI = [-1.12, 1.00]; model of allocentric responses: b = -0.45, 95% BCI = [-1.51, 0.60]).

text.text: In the Hide phase, the participant watched an experimenter hide a ball on the Hide table.
Next, in the Tell phase, the experimenter described the ball's location to the participant.
Finally, in the Seek phase, the experimenter instructed the participant to find a ball hidden "in the same location" on the Seek table, and the participant chose one location to search.
Critically, the experimenter's description of the ball's location during the Tell phase sometimes included co-speech gestures.

The first trials were Gesture trials (n = 8), during which the experimenter's descriptions included co-speech gestures that adopted a specific frame of reference (Gestural FoR condition: Egocentric vs.
Allocentric) to convey the ball's location.
This gestural frame of reference was manipulated between subjects and counterbalanced; speech was scripted and identical between conditions.

If gestures can shape the frame of reference adopted by an observer, then participants should search more often under the cup that is consistent with the frame of reference adopted in the experimenter's gestural description.
On subsequent No Gesture trials (n = 4), the researcher's descriptions were identical except they did not include gesture.
No-Gesture trials assessed whether the effect of the gestural manipulation persisted in the absence of ongoing gestural cues.

Before the start of each trial, a divider was placed to hide the Seek table, and the experimenter set up the Seek table by hiding two balls, one under the cup corresponding to an egocentric search strategy, the other under the cup corresponding to an allocentric search strategy.
Each trial then began with the Hide phase, in which the participant watched the experimenter hide a ball under one of four identical cups arranged in a row on the Hide table (Fig. 3, left).

The experimenter then turned 180º to face the participant for the Tell phase.
The experimenter described the ball's location (Fig. 3, middle) by stating, "On the table behind me, there are four cups.

On Gesture trials, the experimenter accompanied their speech with a series of gestures that represented the ball's location according to a particular frame of reference, either egocentric or allocentric, and we manipulated this gestural FoR between-subjects.
While saying "there are four cups," the experimenter produced a sequence of iconic gestures (hands cupped downward) that depicted the row of four cups.
They accompanied the phrase "this cup" with a gesture that represented the ball's location using either an egocentric or an allocentric FoR.

In the Egocentric condition, the experimenter's gestures represented the ball's location relative to their body (e.g., if they hid the ball to their left, after rotating 180º they gestured to their left).

In the Allocentric condition, the experimenter's gestures represented the ball's location relative to external coordinates (e.g., if they hid the ball to their left, after rotating 180º they gestured to their right).

Finally, in the Seek phase, the divider was removed to reveal the Seek table behind the participant, and the participant rotated 180° to search for a ball on this table by lifting one of four cups (Fig. 3, right).

Recall that, before the start of each trial, while the Seek table was hidden from view behind a divider, an experimenter hid balls under the two cups on the Seek table that were consistent with an egocentric or an allocentric response.

An egocentric response consisted of searching under the cup in the same position from the searcher's perspective (e.g., if the experimenter hid the ball under the rightmost cup, then the participant would search under the rightmost cup).

An allocentric response consisted of searching under the cup in the same position from an external perspective (e.g., if the experimenter hid the ball in the cup closest to the wall, then the participant would search under the cup closest to the wall).
While the participant believed there was only one hidden ball, by actually hiding two balls we allowed the participant to succeed with either an allocentric or an egocentric response.
Once the participant lifted the cup of their choice, either revealing a ball or nothing, the trial ended.
Each session began with Gesture trials (n = 8), followed by No-Gesture trials (n = 4).
No-Gesture trials were procedurally identical to Gesture trials except the experimenter never gestured, and the spoken description changed from "under this cup" to "under a cup."

Allocentric), Trial Type (Gesture vs.
No-Gesture), and their interaction, and random intercepts for participants and items.
In a second Bayesian logistic model, we re-baselined Trial Type on the No Gesture trials where the experimenter did not gesture (trials 9-12).

Two experiments tested whether gestural relativity is a viable mechanism for propagating and perpetuating spatial frames of reference.
Experiment 1 demonstrated that the frame of reference participants adopted in the privacy of their minds surfaced publicly in their gestures.

Experiment 2 investigated whether those public traces were causally consequential for observers' thinking, and found that spatial gestures shape the frame of reference that they use to reason spatially.
Gesture is thus a channel through which spatial frames of reference can be expressed and transmitted.
These results complicate the relation between spatial language, gesture, and thought.

Linguistic relativity holds that habitual language use shapes habitual thought (Whorf, 1956), although evidence is mixed for the case of spatial frames of reference (e.g., Le Guen, 2011; Adamou & Shen, 2017; Calderón et al., 2019; Kısa et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Linguistic relativity holds that habitual language use shapes habitual thought <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Whorf, 1956)</ref>, although evidence is mixed for the case of spatial frames of reference (e.g., Le Guen, 2011; <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Adamou & Shen, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Calderón et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Kısa et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Our results suggest that gesture may be a complementary mechanism.
Just as repeated exposure to frames of reference in spatial language may reinforce those frames of reference in non-linguistic spatial cognition, so too could repeated exposure to spatial gesture.
Gesture may thus function as a "spotlight" (Wolff & Holmes, 2011), repeatedly drawing attention to certain spatial relationships.
text.formatted: Gesture may thus function as a "spotlight" <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Wolff & Holmes, 2011)</ref>, repeatedly drawing attention to certain spatial relationships.

text.text: Over time, repeated exposure to a particular spatial frame of reference in gesture could instill a habitual bias, thus privileging that frame of reference in non-communicative thinking (cf. Amir & Pitt, 2026).

text.text: Future work should investigate the long-term effects of habitual exposure to spatial gesture.

Recall from the Introduction that there are communities in which the habitual frame of reference in speech diverges from the habitual frame of reference in thought (Le Guen, 2011; Marghetis et al., 2020; Calderón et al., 2019).

text.text: Linguistic relativity cannot explain the existence of norms of spatial thinking in these communities.
These divergences between language and thought make sense, however, if norms for spatial thinking are also products of gestural relativity (Le Guen, 2011; Calderón et al., 2019).
text.formatted: These divergences between language and thought make sense, however, if norms for spatial thinking are also products of gestural relativity <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Le Guen, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Calderón et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Yucatec Mayan women, for instance, think allocentrically even though they lack competence with spoken allocentric terms (Le Guen, 2011 ). Le Guen (2011) speculates that this community may rely more on gesture for communicating spatial information because they often need to accurately convey allocentric cardinal directions, and it is easier to convey precise information about angles in gesture than in speech.

Le Guen (2011)</ref> speculates that this community may rely more on gesture for communicating spatial information because they often need to accurately convey allocentric cardinal directions, and it is easier to convey precise information about angles in gesture than in speech.

text.text: This suggests one scenario in which gestural relativity may play an outsized role in transmitting community norms of spatial thinking: When a community values precision in allocentric orientation, norms of spatial thinking may be conveyed more through gesture than through speech.
Gesture is thus one possible mechanism by which a community maintains shared norms of spatial thinking, but it is unlikely to be the only one.
For example, some built environments may favor egocentric thinking (Mishra, Dasen, & Niraula, 2003; Majid et al., 2004; Dasen & Mishra, 2010).
text.formatted: For example, some built environments may favor egocentric thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Mishra, Dasen, & Niraula, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Majid et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Dasen & Mishra, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A study of Tamil speakers in India found that those living in a city favored an egocentric FoR in their thinking while those in rural areas favored an allocentric FoR (Pederson, 1995), and language communities in urban environments are statistically more likely to reason egocentrically (Marghetis, Ortega, & Holmes, 2024).

text.text: Other aspects of material culture may also play a role in regimenting a community's spatial thinking.

The Hai||om of Namibia, for instance, have shifted toward egocentric spatial thinking while their spatial language has remained predominantly allocentric, and this shift in spatial thinking has been hypothesized to reflect exposure to material artifacts such as books, maps, and digital screens (Kısa et al., 2026).

text.text: Community norms of spatial thinking, therefore, are unlikely to reflect a single, isolated cause.
This suggests the need for an ecological perspective that reflects the multicausality of spatial cognition (Marghetis et al., 2020; Palmer et al., 2017; cf., Hutchins, 2010).
text.formatted: This suggests the need for an ecological perspective that reflects the multicausality of spatial cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Marghetis et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Palmer et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">cf., Hutchins, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: An ecological perspective emphasizes how the spatial reasoner is embedded in a broader ecosystem of mutually-constraining practices and resources.

Norms of private spatial thinking may reflect the confluence -and sometimes the conflictof all these factors, including language (Majid et al., 2004; Levinson, 2003; Whorf, 1956), gesture (Le Guen, 2011; Calderón et al., 2019), material artifacts (Kısa et al., 2026), the larger built environment (Marghetis et al., 2024), the natural landscape (Palmer et al., 2017), limitations of visual perception (Pitt et al., 2022), the pragmatics of the task itself (Li & Gleitman, 2002), and innate biases (Haun et al., 2006).

text.text: None of these operate in isolation.

Some may have an outsized role in establishing and sustaining spatial habits -"keystone species" in the ecosystem of spatial thought -and the relative influence of any particular factor may vary between communities.

We speculate that gesture may often occupy a privileged position within this ecosystem because of its intrinsic spatiality and ubiquity in face-to-face interaction, but the full ecology of influences on spatial cognition remains to be characterized.
How are private conventions for thinking about space made public and thus shared?
We have shown that gesture can be part of the answer.

When speakers internalized a local norm for spatial reasoning, they expressed it spontaneously in their gestures; when observers encountered such gestures, they adopted the encoded frame of reference in their own spatial reasoning.
Taken together, these two findings demonstrate the viability of gesture as a mechanism for transmitting community norms of spatial thinking.
Repeated, habitual exposure to frame-of-reference-encoding gestures may transmit and sustain shared spatial preferences within communities.

This suggests that some cross-cultural variation in spatial thinking could be driven by gestural relativity, rather than linguistic relativity, a possibility that should be explored in future field research.

More generally, gestural relativity may be an underappreciated channel of cultural transmission, with cultural norms shaping how people gesture within the community, and exposure to these gestures then biasing observers toward those community norms.
Fig 1: Procedure for Experiment 1.
Participants engaged in two tasks (Cup and Map) across two phases (Training and Test).

(A) The Cup Task involved reproducing a ball's movement from one cup to another.During Training (n = 4 trials, left), participants were exposed to the norm of the micro-community (egocentric or allocentric), manipulated between-subjects.
First the Director modeled a motion trajectory by moving a ball between two cups (e.g., a zig-zag path in the air from the leftmost to the rightmost cup).
The Director then instructed the participant and the Player to rotate 180º and move the ball "the same way."
The Player modeled the normative frame of reference by reproducing the ball's motion according to the normative frame of reference.
If the participant did not adopt the normative frame of reference in their own response, the Director provided generic corrective feedback to follow the Player's lead.
On Test trials (n = 4 trials, right), the participant took over the role of the Director by improvising a motion trajectory for moving the ball from one cup to another.
They then rotated 180º and described the motion event to the Player.
The Player then attempted to reproduce this motion event on the other table, hidden behind an occluding wall so the participant did not receive any feedback.
Participants' gestures while describing their motion trajectory were coded as either egocentric or allocentric.
(B) Motion trajectories during training for the Cup task.
(Red circles = cups; arrows = motion trajectories.) (C) The Map Task involved following an escape route in a maze printed on a large paper placed on the table.
The design was otherwise identical to the Cup Task.

(A) Proportion of trials on which participants gestured allocentrically (left) or egocentrically (right), split by norm condition (egocentric norm = teal circles; allocentric norm = orange triangles).
Local norms increased the proportion of gestures consistent with that norm (error bars indicate standard errors).
(B) An egocentric gesture produced by a participant in the egocentric norm condition.
Before rotating, she had escaped a maze on the table behind her by tracing a path that was oriented to her right.
After rotating, she pointed to her right with one hand while reenacting the rightward motion with her other hand, thus reproducing the motion egocentrically from her perspective.
Note that, from an external allocentric perspective, she had escaped by moving away from the side wall but gestured toward the wall.
(C) An allocentric gesture produced by a participant in the allocentric norm condition.
Before rotating, while facing the table behind her, she had moved a ball from the cup closest to the side wall to the cup farthest from the side wall.
After rotating, she gestured away from the wall, thus reproducing the motion from an external, allocentric perspective.
Note that, from her perspective, she had moved the ball left-to-right but gestured right-to-left.
